stemBlocks.value: Think first: Part a is decimal arithmetic under a fraction bar; part b is a standard-form division where the powers of ten are handled by subtracting indices.

solutionSteps.instruction: Multiply out the numerator of a.

contentBlocks.value: 42 × 7 = 294, with three decimal places in total

solutionSteps.instruction: Split part b into front numbers and powers of ten.
State the ordinary value for b.

strategyBlocks.value: In a, complete the numerator then divide by 2.1; in b, divide the front numbers and subtract the indices.

whyThisWorks.value: Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the indices, because the division cancels matching factors of ten from top and bottom. That lets a standard-form division break cleanly into two independent pieces: a small ordinary division and an index subtraction. In part a the fraction bar again groups the numerator, so the product is finished before any dividing.

commonErrors.misconception: Dividing the indices in part b instead of subtracting them, giving 10².
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Dividing the indices in part b instead of subtracting them, giving 10².

commonErrors.misconception: Dividing 4.2 by 2.1 first and then multiplying by 0.07 — this happens to give the same value here, but it is not what the bar instructs and fails when the numerator is a sum.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Dividing 4.2 by 2.1 first and then multiplying by 0.07 — this happens to give the same value here, but it is not what the bar instructs and fails when the numerator is a sum.

commonErrors.misconception: Losing a decimal place and writing 4.2 × 0.07 as 2.94.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Losing a decimal place and writing 4.2 × 0.07 as 2.94.

examTip.value: For any standard-form product or quotient, deal with the front numbers and the indices in two separate columns — mixing them in one line is where marks disappear.
